sections.heading: Employee ownership: three ways workers can own the company
bullets: An ESOP is a trust that holds shares for employees automatically — broad but indirect. A direct shareholder program sells real stock to selected employees (often financed by stock-backed loans or payroll deduction), concentrating ownership among people making an active commitment
Profit sharing is the third layer: no equity at all, but a slice of annual profits deposited into employees' retirement accounts — often formula-weighted so it matters most to the lowest-paid

Private-company shares need a price without a stock market: an independent annual valuation sets it, and mandatory sell-back windows (e.g., divest between ages 60-65) keep ownership with active workers rather than alumni or outsiders

Corporate form gates all of this: an S corporation is capped at 100 shareholders and excludes non-US owners, so a firm wanting thousands of employee-owners across global offices must convert to a C corporation — a tax trade-off made for ownership reach

sections.heading: Design for manufacture: how prefab actually works
bullets: DfMA (design for manufacture and assembly) means designing the building from day one as kits a factory can produce — wall panels, structural frames, bathroom pods, equipment skids — rather than drawings a field crew interprets

The pipeline is digital end-to-end: the BIM model (e.g., Revit) drives the factory's cutting and framing machines directly, so what's manufactured is exactly what was modeled — no shop-drawing translation loss

A bathroom pod shows the economics: it consolidates the work of roughly eight trades (framing, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing, tile, fixtures...) into one factory product, craned in and connected — one inspection, one warranty, days instead of weeks per room

At AI-campus scale the flagship prefab move is the building envelope: hundreds of insulated metal panels per building installed at 15-20 a day can enclose a half-million-square-foot structure in under eight weeks, letting interior trades start in weather-protected space months early

sections.heading: VDC: building the building twice
bullets: Virtual design and construction (VDC) means fully building the project in software before the field — the BIM model carries every duct, conduit, and hanger, not just architecture

Clash detection is the headline payoff: the software finds every place the sprinkler main runs through the beam before steel is ordered, converting field rework (expensive, scheduled) into model fixes (cheap, instant)
4D adds time: linking model elements to the schedule animates the build sequence, exposing trade-stacking conflicts and crane-logistics problems while they're still plans

After turnover the model becomes a digital twin — a live software mirror of the facility that operations teams use to locate equipment, plan maintenance, and simulate changes; offshore VDC teams make the modeling labor scale globally

sections.heading: Inside an AI data hall: from rack to fabric
bullets: Modern AI buildings are quoted like this: four data halls of 25 MW each = a 100 MW building. Each hall holds hundreds of racks, and a rack-scale AI system (e.g., a 72-GPU liquid-cooled cabinet) can draw over 100 kW — ten times a traditional enterprise rack

The GPUs must train as one machine, so the network fabric — the high-speed switching tying tens of thousands of GPUs together — is as architecturally important as power: a building designed so 100,000 GPUs sit on one fabric minimizes the distance and hops between any two of them

Density drove cooling indoors: at 100+ kW per rack, air can't carry the heat away — liquid loops run to cold plates on the chips, and the building's job becomes delivering chilled liquid and megawatt-scale power to every row

This is why the GC's MEP and commissioning muscle decides the schedule: the shell is finished months before the halls; the long pole is energizing, flushing, and proving the power-and-liquid systems hall by hall

sections.heading: Schedule science: critical path and compression
bullets: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks — the sequence that sets the finish date; everything else has 'float' (slack). Schedule management is really critical-path management

Compression has two levers: fast-tracking (overlapping tasks that normally run in sequence — design and construction, sitework and steel) and crashing (adding resources — double shifts, more crews) — both trade money and risk for time

Prefab compresses structurally: factory work runs in parallel with sitework, off the critical path entirely, then installs in days — which is why heavily prefabricated projects absorb disruptions better

When a delay threatens (a late transformer, a design change), joint re-planning with subs and suppliers can re-sequence around it — the difference between a five-month slip and a four-week one is usually planning agility, not heroics

sections.heading: Safety systems and their limits on the megasite
bullets: US sites are governed by OSHA standards (fall protection, excavation shoring, equipment-operator training); citations carry modest dollar penalties but real reputational weight, and can be contested or settled — a withdrawn citation is a negotiated outcome, not an exoneration or a conviction

Heat is the megasite killer in Sun Belt construction: prevention is engineered (shade, water, rest cycles, acclimatization schedules), and its absence shows up in emergency-call logs before it shows up in injury statistics

The industry's report cards are EMR (insurance-derived experience modifier; 1.0 is average) and TRIR/DART incident rates — but they're self-reported or insurer-held, and a contractor that publishes awards while declining to share rates is choosing opacity a sophisticated client will notice

Scale itself is a risk factor: thousands of workers from dozens of subcontractors, 60-hour weeks, and NDA-bound labor forces make information flow — the raw material of safety management — hardest exactly where the stakes are highest

flashcards.q: What's the difference between an ESOP and a direct shareholder ownership program?
flashcards.a: An ESOP is a trust holding shares for all employees automatically — broad but indirect. A direct program sells real stock to selected employees (financed via stock-backed loans, payroll deduction, or options), concentrating ownership among people making an active buy-in commitment.

flashcards.q: How does a private company set its share price with no stock market?
flashcards.a: An independent valuation firm appraises the company annually and that becomes the transaction price for all buys and sell-backs. Mandatory divestment windows (e.g., sell down between ages 60-65) keep ownership with active employees rather than retirees or outsiders.

flashcards.q: Why would an employee-owned firm convert from an S corporation to a C corporation?
flashcards.a: S-corps are capped at 100 shareholders and exclude non-US-citizen/resident owners. A firm wanting thousands of employee-owners across international offices must convert to a C-corp — accepting different taxation to remove the ownership ceiling.

Design for Manufacture and Assembly: designing the building from the start as factory-producible kits — wall panels, structural frames, pods, skids — with the BIM model driving factory machines directly, rather than producing drawings for field crews to interpret.

flashcards.q: Why is a factory-built bathroom pod such a big productivity win?
flashcards.a: It consolidates roughly eight trades — framing, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing, tile, fixtures — into one product built on an assembly line, then craned in and connected. One installation, one inspection, days instead of weeks per room, and the site never sequences those eight trades.

flashcards.q: What is clash detection in VDC/BIM?
flashcards.a: Software comparison of every modeled system to find physical conflicts — the sprinkler main routed through a steel beam — before anything is fabricated. It converts expensive, schedule-eating field rework into cheap, instant model fixes.

flashcards.q: What does '4D' mean in construction modeling, and what is a digital twin?
flashcards.a: 4D links the 3D model to the schedule, animating the build sequence to expose trade-stacking and logistics conflicts in advance. After turnover, the model lives on as a digital twin — a software mirror of the real facility used for operations, maintenance, and change planning.

flashcards.q: Why do AI racks need liquid cooling when older data centers used air?
flashcards.a: A rack-scale AI system (e.g., a 72-GPU liquid-cooled cabinet) draws 100+ kW — roughly 10x a traditional enterprise rack. Air physically can't carry heat away fast enough at that density, so liquid loops run to cold plates on the chips, and the building delivers chilled liquid to every row.

flashcards.q: What is the 'network fabric' of an AI campus and why does it shape building design?
flashcards.a: The high-speed switching layer that ties tens of thousands of GPUs into one training machine. Since every GPU must talk to every other with minimal latency, buildings are designed so as many GPUs as possible share one fabric — making network topology an architectural driver, not an IT afterthought.

flashcards.q: What is the critical path of a project, and what is 'float'?
flashcards.a: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks — it alone sets the finish date. Every other task has float (slack it can slip without delaying completion). Schedule management is really about protecting and compressing the critical path.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between fast-tracking and crashing a schedule?
flashcards.a: Fast-tracking overlaps tasks that normally run in sequence (design with construction, sitework with steel design) — trading design certainty for time. Crashing adds resources (double shifts, extra crews) — trading money for time. Both add risk; prefab compresses without either by moving work off the critical path into parallel factory production.

flashcards.q: What are EMR and TRIR, and what are their limits as safety evidence?
flashcards.a: EMR is an insurance-derived experience modifier (1.0 = industry average — it directly prices a contractor's workers' comp); TRIR/DART are recordable-injury rates per 100 workers. Both are self-reported or insurer-held: a firm can publish safety awards while declining to disclose its rates, and emergency-call logs or citations may tell a different story than the marketing.
